 View CCSS | NGSS Most North Americans will move their clocks back an hour on Nov 1 (Credit: Worldtimewise.com) It is that time of the year again! On November 1, 2026, many North Americans will add 60 minutes to their weekend by turning their clocks back an hour. This simple action marks the end of Daylight Saving Time (DST), which began on March 8, 2026. The time change will help shift more sunlight back into the morning and make it a little easier to wake up for school or work during the shorter winter days ahead.
 DST was first introduced during World War I. In 1916, the German Empire moved clocks forward by one hour to reduce the need for artificial lighting and save fuel for the war effort. The US and Britain soon followed. After the war, all the countries reverted to Standard Time only to reinstate DST during World War II.
 DST was first implemented in the United States to conserve energy during World War I (Credit: United Cigar Stores Company/ Public domain/ Wikimedia Commons) When the war ended in 1945, US officials canceled DST nationwide , but allowed states and districts to continue the practice . They could even set their own start and stop dates. This resulted in a confusing patchwork of different schedules. By 1965, just Iowa had 23 different sets of DST start and end dates. 
 The Uniform Time Act of 1966 ended this confusion by setting the same "spring forward" and "fall back" dates for the entire country. But the law was not mandatory . As a result, Hawaii, most of Arizona, along with several US territories, chose not to adopt the time change.
 DST initially began and ended on the last Sundays in April and October. However, in 1986, President Ronald Reagan moved the DST start date to the first Sunday in April. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 changed it again, this time to the second Sunday in March. It also extended the DST end date to the first Sunday in November. The new schedule took effect in 2007 and is still used today.
 Many states have tried to pass laws to stop the time change (Credit: Statista/ CC BY-SA 2.0) Though the dates vary , about 70 countries around the world observe DST. But the biannual clock change has always been controversial. Experts say the time changes disrupt the body’s sleep-wake cycle. This can lead to fatigue , reduced concentration , and even an increased risk of heart problems.
 Over the years, several US states have passed laws to stay on DST year-round. However, those laws cannot take effect unless federal law changes. That could happen soon if Congress passes the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make DST permanent nationwide. The House passed the bill by a vote of 308–117 in July 2026, but the Senate has yet to approve it. So, for now, unless you live in a state that does not observe DST, you have no choice but to enjoy the bonus hour on November 1.
 Happy "Fall Back!"
